subject: community-medicine
title: Sanitary Awakening to Alma-Ata: Chadwick, Lister, Ross and Primary Health Care

steps.title: Industrial cities at their unhealthiest
steps.tx: The **industrial revolution** created slums, overcrowding, accumulated filth and high sickness and death rates, especially among women and children. In 1842 the mean age at death in London was 44 years for gentry and professionals but only 22 years for the working class. Frequent cholera visitations compounded the misery and forced the state to look at living conditions.
steps.say: Industrial growth poisoned its own cities. Slums, crowding and filth drove death rates up, and in 1842 Londoners of the working class died at a mean age of twenty two against forty four for professionals. Cholera forced official attention.

steps.title: Chadwick and the great sanitary awakening
steps.tx: **Edwin Chadwick**, a lawyer, investigated the health of large town inhabitants after the cholera epidemic of 1832. His report on the sanitary conditions of the labouring population in Great Britain became a landmark of public health, focusing government attention on housing and working conditions. Filth was named man's greatest enemy, and the anti-filth crusade that followed is called the great sanitary awakening.
steps.say: A lawyer changed medicine here. After the 1832 cholera epidemic he documented how the labouring population lived, and his report forced housing and working conditions onto the government agenda. Filth was named the enemy; the crusade became the great sanitary awakening.

steps.tx: The great sanitary awakening was started by a lawyer. After the cholera epidemic of 1832, **Edwin Chadwick** investigated how labouring people in large towns were housed and how they worked. His report on sanitary conditions in Great Britain made government attend to those conditions. He called filth man's greatest enemy. The street of crowding, open waste and a shared pump is the subject of that report, not a hospital interior, because the enemy he named lived outside the ward.
steps.say: After cholera in 1832, Edwin Chadwick, a lawyer, documented the housing and working conditions of labouring people in Britain's large towns. His sanitary report put those conditions in front of government. He named filth the greatest enemy, and the campaign that followed is the great sanitary awakening.

steps.title: The Public Health Acts and state duty
steps.tx: The **Public Health Act of 1848** in England first enacted the principle that the state holds direct responsibility for the health of the people. Sir John Simon, first medical officer of health for London, then built a public health system admired worldwide. The comprehensive Public Health Act of 1875 consolidated control of the physical environment, from water to housing.
steps.say: Law converted outrage into duty. The 1848 Act made the state responsible for public health for the first time. London's first medical officer of health built the admired system, and the 1875 Act consolidated control over water, housing and environment.

steps.title: Lister and antiseptic surgery
steps.tx: **Joseph Lister** applied the germ theory to the operating theatre, using carbolic acid antisepsis to kill microbes in wounds, instruments and dressings. Surgical sepsis, once expected after operations, fell sharply, and amputation mortality dropped with it. His work turned Pasteur's laboratory insight into a daily hospital ritual: sterile technique, later refined from antisepsis toward asepsis.
steps.say: Germ theory entered the operating theatre through carbolic acid. Wounds, instruments and dressings were treated to kill microbes, surgical sepsis fell, and amputation deaths dropped. Laboratory insight became daily ritual, later refined from antisepsis toward asepsis.

steps.title: Ronald Ross and the mosquito proof
steps.tx: **Ronald Ross** proved in 1897 that Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria, finding the parasite's developmental stages in the mosquito gut at Secunderabad. Vector control thereby gained a scientific target: drain breeding sites, screen houses and attack the insect, not only the patient. His Nobel Prize in 1902 marked vector borne disease as a public health discipline.
steps.say: In 1897 a surgeon major in India found malaria parasites developing inside Anopheles mosquitoes, proving the vector. Control gained a target beyond the patient: breeding sites, house screening and the insect itself. A Nobel Prize followed in 1902.

steps.title: Health for All and the 1977 resolution
steps.tx: The **World Health Assembly** resolved in 1977 that the main social goal of governments and the World Health Organization should be attainment by all people, by the year 2000, of a level of health permitting a socially and economically productive life. That goal, Health for All, answered the gross disparities between rich and poor, urban and rural populations.
steps.say: A global goal replaced scattered programmes in 1977. Governments pledged that by 2000 everyone would reach health permitting a socially and economically productive life. Health for All answered the gross gaps between rich and poor, city and village.

steps.title: Alma-Ata and the definition of primary care
steps.tx: The **Alma-Ata declaration** of 1978 defined primary health care as essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods, made universally accessible through full community participation at a cost the community and country can afford. It called this approach health by the people, placing people's health in people's hands.
steps.say: One year later a conference in Alma-Ata named the vehicle. Essential care, scientifically sound and socially acceptable, universally accessible through community participation, at affordable cost. Health by the people became the slogan, and the definition still anchors exams.

steps.title: Eight elements and four principles
steps.tx: **Primary health care** rests on equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination and appropriate technology. Its eight elements run from education about prevailing health problems, food supply and nutrition, safe water and sanitation, maternal and child health with family planning, immunisation and endemic disease control, to treatment of common conditions and essential drugs.
steps.say: Four principles carry the system: equity, participation, intersectoral coordination and appropriate technology. Eight elements fill it, from health education and safe water to maternal care, immunisation, endemic control, common treatment and essential drugs.

steps.tx: **Primary health care** stands on equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination and appropriate technology. The eight elements are education on the prevailing health problems, food supply and nutrition, safe water and sanitation, maternal and child health including family planning, immunisation, control of endemic disease, treatment of common conditions, and essential drugs. The centre in the middle of the diagram is where that list is delivered, close to where people live, rather than a distant specialist hospital.
steps.say: Four principles hold primary health care: equity, community participation, work across sectors, and technology that fits the setting. Eight elements fill the list, from health education, food, safe water and maternal care to immunisation, endemic disease control, ordinary treatment and essential drugs.

steps.title: From disease control phase to comprehensive care
steps.tx: The early **disease control phase** of public health, roughly 1880 to 1920, chased general cleanliness, garbage disposal and quarantine. Alma-Ata widened that narrow start into comprehensive care joining promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative services at the first contact level. Exams contrast the two eras to test whether candidates see public health as sanitation alone or as a full system.
steps.say: Close with the widening arc. Early public health chased cleanliness, garbage and quarantine. Alma-Ata widened that start into comprehensive first contact care: promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative together. Sanitation alone is the old answer; the system is the new one.
